captions.instagram:
What is Snell's law of refraction?

Why does a straw look broken in a glass of water? Bend a laser across a boundary and watch Snell's law at work, then find the same rule in shallow-looking pools, prisms and rainbows, camera lenses and your own eye, diamonds and the glass fibres of the internet, and the mirage on a hot road.

→ Light bends when it enters a slower material. Snell’s law: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.
→ From glass into air, tilt past 41.8° and no light escapes. It all reflects back.
→ A straw looks broken because light bends leaving the water. Your eye sees it higher.
→ In every raindrop, sunlight bends, reflects and bunches up at 42°. That’s the rainbow.
→ In your eye the cornea does two thirds of the bending. Under water it almost stops.

youtubeLong.title: What is Snell's law of refraction? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Why does a straw look broken in a glass of water? Bend a laser across a boundary and watch Snell's law at work, then find the same rule in shallow-looking pools, prisms and rainbows, camera lenses and your own eye, diamonds and the glass fibres of the internet, and the mirage on a hot road.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/snellclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/snellclear

In this video:
• Light bends when it changes speed. Every material slows light by a factor n, its refractive index: v = c ÷ n.
• Your eyes are fooled every day. Things under water look higher than they are, so straws look broken and pools look three quarters as deep.
• Lenses are Snell's law, twice. Curved glass bends each ray by just the right amount to bring them to one focus.
• Past the critical angle, light is trapped. Going into a faster material, beyond sin θc = n₂ ÷ n₁ nothing gets out: total internal reflection, a perfect mirror.
• Mirages, negative index, and a myth. Hot air over a road curves sky light upwards into a fake puddle.
